en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhànruán of Bīlíng during the Táng Dynasty.
This work follows [the previous text] to clarify the Great Impurity (mahā-aśubha). First, the distinct names are presented.

Regarding the statement "as previously distinguished," this refers to the fact that while the preceding section dealt with the Minor Impurity, the subsequent section clarifies the *prātikūlya-vimokṣa* (liberation through repulsiveness); these together constitute the whole.
The two vehicles are distinct from the bodhisattvas;
now, the "Great Impurity" is likewise so.
Next, in the formal explanation, the characteristics are first shown.
"Qiu" means a mound;
it is a small hill.
"Mu" means a tomb; it is a grave.
The *Book of Rites* states:
"Generally, a burial site that has no mound is called a *mu*.
The *Baihutong* states:
The tomb of a Son of Heaven is three *ren* high.
One *ren* is seven feet.
It is planted with pine trees.
The feudal lords used half that height, planting cypress trees;
the great officers used eight chi, planting *luán* trees.
Regarding the *luán*, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: [it is a type of tree].
It resembles a wooden railing.
For the *shi*, four feet in height, they plant *huai* trees;
for the commoners (*shu ren*), there are no mounds, and they plant willows and poplars.
Thus we know that tombs are common to both the noble and the humble.
*Wang* means "deep water.
The *Guangya* states:
It is like ten thousand *qīng* of ponds.
Regarding the statement that "soup is foul liquid and the like," this refers to the thirteenth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.
Because Kāśyapa challenged the Buddha, saying:
"Such contemplation yields no real benefit;
it is just like when a bhikṣu contemplates impurity."
One perceives the clothes one wears as being entirely like skin,
though they are not actually skin;
and whatever one eats and drinks, one regards it all as insects.
One contemplates fine, delicious soup as being foul-smelling liquid;
one contemplates the food one eats as being like marrow and brain;
one contemplates crushed bones as being like flour.
The characteristics of the formal arousal of the mind while seated are clearly explained below.
Next is the analogy,
as in the text.
The initial contemplation below explains the cultivation and the manifestation [of the path], as in the text.
Furthermore, the section beginning with "Next, all... clarifies the reasons for the transformation of the object.
Because it is transformed by the mind,
two conditions are cited as examples to illustrate that the objects of perception and the resulting fruits differ,
such as in the case of the contemplation of impurity and so forth.
The ripening of the fruit is the power of past mental force;
impurity is the power of present mental force.
Now it is clarified that the manifestation of the signs also arises from past causes.
Although the past and present differ, they are both equally created by the mind.
Therefore, the case of Śreṇika holding stones and other objects serves as an illustration;
it is like the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra’s account of Śreṇika, who perceived all pebbles and rubble as being entirely composed of jewels.
This, too, is brought about by the power of past mental force.
The intention behind what Saṃgharakṣita saw is likewise so.
That sūtra says:
In Śrāvastī, there were five hundred merchants who wished to go to sea to gather treasures.
An elder addressed the group, saying, "I have a teacher of mine named Saṃgharakṣita; you may invite him to be your guide."
They all went together to invite him.
Saṃgharakṣita said,
"You may inform the Upādhyāya Śāriputra."
He then went to where Śāriputra was and informed him.
Śāriputra, in turn, went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha then granted him permission to depart.
They then entered the sea together, but before they had reached the place of treasures,
a nāga king emerged from the ocean.
The people said:
"Who are you, O deity?
The Naga King manifested his form and said,
"Give me Saṃgharakṣita."
The merchants then went with him to the place where the treasures were located.
Upon returning to the spot where their guide had perished, they spoke these words:
"When we reach the presence of the World-Honored One, what should we say?"
The Dragon King, knowing that the merchants were returning, immediately returned Saṃgharakṣita to them.
Thereupon, the merchants returned together with Saṃgharakṣita;
however, being greedy for a shorter route, they chose to return by land.
The merchant set out at night and, by mistake,
abandoned Saṃgharakṣita. Losing his companions,
he traveled alone until he reached a monastery, where he immediately beheld the Saṃghātapati Hell.
The monk entered and was burned by fire.
He asked, "Who is this person?"
He replied:
"The people of Jambudvīpa find it difficult to believe you; you should ask the Buddha about this.
In this manner, one successively sees fifty-three hells."
Having arrived, he questioned the Buddha, who then explained it for him:
"As for the Hell of the Warm Bathhouse,
during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, one used the monastic utensils at will."
Regarding the Gandhabba Hell:
it is so named because [the offender] did not strike the ghaṇṭā (wooden clapper) due to misappropriating the property of the Saṃgha.

Among the monks, there was a senior elder (sthavira) who possessed neither meditative concentration nor discipline;
he would eat his fill and sleep, engaging in worldly talk,
eating fine food for himself while distributing the poor quality to the rest of the community.
The *karmadāna* first eats the coarse portions himself, while those distributed among the monks are likewise of such a nature that they cause suffering.
As for the hell of the "meat-jars scorched by fire":
When serving as the kitchen attendant for the Sangha, one might set aside food for the morning meal until evening;
what was left over in the evening is then kept until the following day.
It is likewise when a donor sends food: it is hidden away and waited upon until the guests have departed.
The same applies to the uneven distribution of monastic fruits.
As for the hell of those who burn others with knives and the cutting off of noses by fire:
Because he spat upon the pure ground of the Sangha,
he was reborn in the Hell of the Flesh-Hammer.
Because he nailed his own robes and alms bowl to the wall of the Sangha's quarters, he was reborn in the Hell of the Nails.
As for the Hell of the Burning Meat-Stand:
one will be born there because one provided bedding and door-bolts for wandering monks,
thereby obstructing the Sangha’s use of them.
To dwell oneself in a fine house while giving inferior ones to others—
suffering is likewise so.
This refers to those who burn houses in hell.
Dwelling in the monastic quarters as if they were one's own,
because one does not shift or divide them according to the sequence [of seniority],
one is reborn in the hell of burning beds.
Because they used the monastic beds without distributing them according to the Dharma,
the wooden frame of the bed broke and caught fire;
their suffering was likewise so.
In the Hell of Burning Bedding, the denizens are burned because they stepped upon the requisites of the Sangha with their feet.
In the Hell of Burning Flesh Toilets, they are likewise burned.
Those who urinate or defecate on pure ground will have their bodies burned by fire while sitting upon high thrones in hell;
those who explain the Vinaya erroneously will likewise suffer there.
They preach the Dharma for the sake of benefit.
Suffering is likewise so.
As for those in the hell of the burning fruit trees:
Because I ate the fruits of the Sangha and [the property] of laypeople,
and because I consumed the four types of meat, I am cast into the Hell of Burning Trees;
this is due to my lack of virtue and the severing of wholesome roots, which renders me unequal [to others].
The suffering of providing bedding for the Saṃgha is likewise.
These two śrāmaṇeras are those who were burned by fire within their robes in hell.
Because the śrāmaṇeras were lying there embracing one another,
that sūtra— still for the sake of benefiting the donors and the bhikṣus—
states: "Even though such a bhikṣu does not uphold the precepts..."
If one obtains such great fruits even by making offerings of the four requisites,
how much more so by making offerings to the Saṃgha of the four directions?
Hells such as these exist everywhere along the shores of the ocean islands.
Or [the same substance] may manifest as a bed, a forest, a water jar, and so forth.
One should know that all material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) accord with the karmic perceptions of individuals;
matter has no fixed essence, but changes according to the mind.
If the contemplation of phenomena is perfected, one is able to transform matter in all cases.
If one maintains that lower-level luminosity possesses the power to destroy fetters because it transforms through its object, [this is incorrect].
Regarding the statement that this contemplation accords with the path of transformation:
if the mental visualization is perfected,
one will truly perceive all objects as transforming into impurity.
Just as a person with supernormal powers causes actual transformation of objects,
one who transforms objects through conceptual imagination attains a power similar to theirs;
therefore, it is said that they have realized the way of transformative change.
Furthermore, within all things there exists the principle of transformability;
therefore, those with supernormal powers and practitioners of contemplation are able to effect such transformations.
This principle is fundamentally the inconceivable dharma within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Following the mind’s grasping, things become external and limited;
yet the path of the bodhisattvas you practice is such that the equal dharma-realm is not diminished by even a single square inch.
If one distinguishes between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) regarding the fundamental [dhyānas], those that are exclusively tainted have already been explained as before.
This includes the minor and major impurities (*aśubha*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so forth.
Although these are objects of uncontaminated [cognition], they are not themselves uncontaminated.
When one correctly employs wisdom to sever afflictions,
because it relies upon a specific stage, it is said that "everything from that stage upward is eliminated."
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that "the path proceeds through nine stages.
As for the phrase "if a person," etc., it refers to a person who, at the lower level, clarifies the liberations (*vimokṣa*) by means of the great impurity (*mahā-aśubha*).
"If a person" and so forth [means]:
From beginning to end, both the primary and secondary retributions are simultaneously subverted.
As for the subsequent section, it discusses the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) by means of the stages of liberation (*vimokṣa*).
First, the heading:
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that being superior to the afflictions is what is called a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Because they are unattached to both the environment (*bhājana-loka*) and its inhabitants (*sattva-loka*),
they possess mastery over the transformation of the environment and its inhabitants.
As the *Mahā-śāstra* states below, it cites the treatise to explain the faculties (*indriya*).
In the Chan school, it is said:
"To complete the cultivation of the liberations (vimokṣa) and then separately cultivate the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) is for those of inferior capacity."
If one were to explain them according to the middle way as in the present text,
there would be no further separate clarification of the initial cultivation of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*);
rather, they would simply be included within the third liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Observing that the first two liberations (vimokṣa) already constitute four of the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana),
and that the third liberation subsequently constitutes the remaining four spheres of mastery,
there is no need to cultivate them separately.
If one possesses superior faculties,
it is not necessary to wait until the conclusion of the third [stage] before once again practicing the two previous liberations (vimokṣa) as the first four.
In the first liberation,
one is able to discern whether things are many or few, beautiful or ugly,
and thus achieves two spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Next, following this, one accomplishes the remaining spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
These are likewise distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior according to the teachings;
they are explained by way of the liberations (*vimokṣa*) to clarify the method of contemplation.
If one possesses the highest of superior faculties, there is no need to rely on the methods for the three grades of faculties.
For example, according to the eighteenth fascicle of the *Sūtra of King Aśoka*, there was a man in the kingdom of Mathurā who left home to become a monk under Kukkuta.
Having heard the teaching on the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), he considered himself to have accomplished what was to be done.
Later, while traveling to the kingdom of Kaṇḍala, he saw a woman and a desire arose within him;
he immediately took the flour from his own alms bowl and gave it to her.
When the woman saw him, she bared her teeth and laughed;
she too conceived lustful thoughts toward the bhikṣu.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu proceeded to contemplate his own body until he saw it as nothing more than a skeleton of teeth.
Having completed the visualization of the bones, one attains arhatship;
that "from many or few, even down to the beautiful and the ugly, all are impure" precisely clarifies the manifestation of the arising [of the sign].
First, the actual clarification of the manifestation;
second, the determination of the stages.
Regarding the first section:
Based on the first liberation (vimokṣa), two spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are established.
"Great trichiliocosm" refers to the many; "decreased" refers to the few.
Such quantities, whether many or few, all possess both beauty and ugliness.
Up to the very last [stage], both the beautiful and the ugly are entirely impure.
Although one contemplates pure forms within the preceding liberations (*vimokṣa*), they are all in fact impure;
yet, one has not yet been able to successively compare and determine the relative beauty and ugliness of these forms.
Because one now observes and knows them well, it is called "superior knowledge" and so forth.
Furthermore, this directly concerns the minor impurities,
clarifying beauty and ugliness solely by relying on the primary retribution (the physical body).
If one gives rise to the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) based on the great impurity,
one likewise attains superior knowledge and vision regarding both the primary and secondary retributions;
this is as explained in detail in the separate teaching on the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
If one establishes two spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) based on the second liberation (vimokṣa) regarding internal inferior [forms],
first the characteristics of their arising are clarified,
and next knowledge and vision are explained.
Next is the determination of the stages.
If one excels in the lower [stages], this clarifies their functional capacity;
in the upper [stages], it cites actual instances.
Regarding those who abdicated their positions and yielded their states:
for example, Wu Taibo was the eldest son of Tai Wang,
while Zhongyong was his younger brother.
His younger brother was Ji Li.
When King Tai fell ill, he yielded the position of heir apparent to his brother and thus excused himself by claiming to gather medicinal herbs, entering into Eastern Wu.
The remainder is as explained in the section on "Aids to the Path.
Regarding the "returning of the oxen" and so forth:
when Yao invited Xu You to serve as the governor of the Nine Provinces, [Xu You declined].
Upon hearing this, he went to the river to wash his ears.
Chao Fu happened to be there tending to his ox when he saw him and asked:
"The lady washes her face first;
why do you wash your ears?
He replied:
"Yao appointed me as the leader of the Nine Provinces.
Fearing that my reputation would spread, I washed it away. Chaofu said:
I have heard that the wood of the *yuzhang* tree grows upon the summits of deep mountains;
above, there is no road for passing carts,
and below, there is no path for crossing perilous terrain.
Though a craftsman may be skillful, he cannot obtain it.
If you wish to avoid the world, why not hide yourself deeply?
Instead, you wander through the human realm, seeking fame and profit in vain.
"I wish to give the ox water to drink, but it will sully its mouth.
Thereupon, he led the ox upstream and gave it water.
Furthermore, in the *Vibhāṣā*, it is asked:
Upon what kind of body are the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) attained?
Answer: They are attained upon a body belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Question:
Can one render the Buddha’s body impure?
Answer: No.
It can be accomplished;
however, only a Buddha is capable of this, and not other śrāvakas and the like.
The Buddha’s body is free from defilement.
Those who practice all forms of the contemplation of impurity cannot conceive of the Buddha’s body as impure.
[This applies to] the three knowledges (trividyā) and the latter four spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
First, the correspondence with the stages;
next, the clarification of the Great and Small Vehicles;
and finally, the distinction between the provisional and the real.
Regarding the "blue, yellow, and so forth" mentioned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
while the latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) involve only four colors,
what is the intention behind listing eight colors here?
Answer: Since the sūtras and śāstras differ, the present text lists them both;
therefore, I shall now provide a judgment.
Blue and so forth arise from substantiality, while earth and so forth arise from conventionality;
this is a judgment regarding the objects of mental focus within samādhi,
and does not refer to the forms apprehended by the five sense faculties.
Therefore, what is seen through samādhi throughout the ten directions is entirely of four colors;
thus, these four colors are real.
If one sees the earth and so forth, they too are these four colors.
Furthermore, because the four names such as "earth" and so forth are established anew,
they are conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
This is because one perceives the eight types of form through the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
If one speaks only of the eight types of form, then both are described according to their substantial reality (*dravya*).
However, when distinguishing the forms perceived by the five sense faculties,
one should state that colors such as blue are conventional (*prajñapti*), while the earth and other elements are substantial.
As the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The great elements (mahābhūta) refer to the four constituents, namely earth, water, fire, and wind;
they perform the functions of supporting and so forth, and possess the natures of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion."
This clarifies that these are the four great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) in their substantial sense.
Their functions—supporting and so forth—clarify the activity of the four great elements;
that is to say, earth performs the function of supporting.
"Et cetera" (ādi) means that it includes the remaining three elements, water and so forth;
namely, water accomplishes cohesion, fire accomplishes heat, and wind accomplishes growth.
Next, it says:
"Earth" refers to manifest color and shape, named according to worldly convention;
the same applies to water and fire.
Wind is likewise both an element and so forth.
Since it is said that these are "worldly conceptions," both shape and manifest color are entirely conventional designations.
Manifest color refers to blue and so forth;
shape refers to squareness and so forth.
Since water and fire also possess both the colors of shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) and manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), it is said that they are likewise.
Regarding wind,
the treatise says:
The wind element is invisible and cannot be seen.
Some say that it is likewise, just like water and fire.
This refers to black winds, circular winds, and so forth.
Regarding these conventional and substantial forms,
among the five sense faculties, conventional form is apprehended by visual consciousness.
Substantial form is that which is apprehended by body-consciousness;
however, what is seen through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not apprehended by either body- or eye-consciousness.
Therefore, there is this distinction between the provisional and the substantial.
Moreover, the blue earth and so forth perceived in samādhi are each seen distinctly without confusion;
this is unlike the *Abhidharmakośa*, which [asserts that they arise] merely upon the basis of real dharmas such as earth.
There are instances where there is manifest color and shape, yet no distinct earth element;
therefore, they are not the same. Thus, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* states:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* simply mentions "blue" and so forth, while the *Mālā* mentions "earth" and so forth;
this distinction is also irrelevant.
The four colors are the names, while "earth" and so forth are the substance.
The name is a mere designation, while the substance is the actual entity.
That text still speaks of "resistant form," making such a statement.
Yet it does not say that these are what is seen through samādhi.
Therefore, we know that "stopping" (śamatha) and "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) are spoken of from the perspective of what is seen within samādhi.
If samādhi is perfected, one sees throughout the ten directions all things that are without form or color.
If light and momentum have not yet been established, there would be both color and shape;
since they are determined based on their establishment, there should be only color.
Although this present text lists both the provisional and the real together, [the distinction remains].
One must maintain the four [bases of mastery] to enter into the four [elements].
These four, together with the preceding four, constitute the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Regarding these four, the presence or absence of the objective phenomena will be explained below.
Regarding the exhaustion of internal and external forms:
one's own skeleton is internal,
while the skeletons of others are external.
Since there is neither internal nor external, and only the eight types of color exist, there is no distinction between beauty and ugliness.
As for the claim that there is only a matter of degree:
although the skeleton may be exhausted, it is not the case that the eight types of color are exhausted.
Regarding the phrase "more or less," it refers to the breadth or narrowness of the eight colors.
Next, to clarify the ten *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities),
first there is a brief determination of their stages.
Among the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), having excluded the first four,
one contemplates both the provisional and the real within the latter four;
therefore, they are said to be eight.
